The US Federal Communications Commission is reported to be drafting a rule that would block imports of Chinese optical transceivers used in data centres.
An optical transceiver is a finger-sized part that links one server to another over fibre inside the building, and one Chinese company, Zhongji Innolight, holds about 27% of that market.

@@REF@@Trump administration drafting ban on Chinese data centre devices, sources say (ChinaTechNews, 2026-08-04)|https://www.chinatechnews.com/2026/08/04/126702-trump-administration-drafting-ban-on-chinese-data-center-devices-sources-say

## What exactly gets blocked
The rule does not reach the parts already plugged in.

According to the reports, it targets models that still have to be authorised.
The FCC controls the authorisation any communications device needs before it can be sold in the US, and it can close the door simply by withholding that authorisation from one supplier's new products.
The same agency used that lever on Chinese networking gear last month, and the ban on Chinese humanoid robot imports this site covered earlier went through the same door.
No provision for ripping out installed equipment has been reported.
So this is less a switch that cuts supply than a device that shortens the list of parts a buyer may choose next.

Adding data centre capacity also means buying more of this one part.|Carl Lender · CC BY 2.0|https://commons.wikimedia.org/wiki/File:Datacenter_Server_Racks_(22370909788).jpg

@@TIME@@2026-06-08|Pentagon adds Zhongji Innolight to its list of firms tied to China's military|2026-07-30|Hong Kong debut closes below the offer price after a $6.8bn raise|2026-08-04|Reports of an FCC draft rule blocking optical transceiver imports|>Within 2026|Rule expected to be published and take effect@@Listing, flotation and draft rule fell into one line within two months. The share sale sat in the middle of it.@@US Federal Register (2026-06-10) · Caixin Global (2026-07-31) · ChinaTechNews (2026-08-04)

## The weight behind 27%
The company raised $6.8bn listing in Hong Kong last month, the city's largest flotation since 2019.
It closed its first day below the offer price, in a week when doubts about AI spending were spreading across the whole market.

One way to read that is that the market had already marked down the company's American revenue.
In June the Pentagon put the company on its list of firms tied to China's military.
That list only bars defence procurement and has no direct hold on commercial data centres, and this rule is an attempt to move the same line into the commercial market.

## The gap Coherent and Lumentum do not close
Blocking and replacing are different jobs.

@@REF@@Trump eyes ban on Chinese data centre components (StratNews Global, 2026-08-04)|https://stratnewsglobal.com/world-news/trump-eyes-ban-on-chinese-data-centre-components/|https://stratnewsglobal.com/wp-content/uploads/2026/08/China-2026-08-04T163641.501.png

That report names Coherent and Lumentum as the American firms that would inherit the space, and carries the analysts' view alongside it: neither yet has the manufacturing scale to replace Chinese output in full.
Factories grow more slowly than rules do. Ordering tools, installing them and getting yields right takes a length of time that has nothing to do with a publication schedule.
Data centres keep going up in the meantime.

## What to watch at Zhongji Innolight after August
The fork is whether the draft becomes a rule at all, and whether a clause covering already installed gear is attached when it does.
If installed equipment is caught, the company's American revenue falls by more than the market has priced.
If the line holds at new models only, what shrinks is the growth rate rather than the money coming in today.
Either way the party paying is the data centre operator, and component prices start moving before any rule is settled.

Share here is counted in money taken, not in units shipped.

If prices are heading down, whoever signed first wins; if prices are heading up, whoever signed later wins.
This is the second case.
The maker that locked in supply earliest appears to have carried the lowest fixed prices through the quarter for exactly that reason.

Apacer is a Taiwanese memory module maker. It buys finished chips and sells them as the sticks that go into machines, which puts it at the back of the allocation queue.
Its CEO said the DRAM that module makers receive in 2027 could drop to roughly 30% of this year's volume.
About 60% of DRAM capacity now goes to servers, and consumer products divide what is left.

@@IMG@@https://upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/3/3e/DDR5_SDRAM_%28with_scale%29_IMGP6298_smial_wp.jpg/960px-DDR5_SDRAM_%28with_scale%29_IMGP6298_smial_wp.jpg|A DRAM stick for a server. ## What does sold out actually mean
It does not mean there is nothing to buy. It means the order of who gets served first is already fixed.

Memory makers are shipping only 60% to 70% of the volumes buyers asked for.
A company that requested 100 receives 65.
Cloud providers and AI firms are filled first, smartphone and PC makers come next.
Module houses stand behind them, and the 30% figure from Apacer is the view from the end of that line.

One more thing follows from this.
A company that has not locked its volumes knows that stepping in now would shrink the allocations of firms already served.
So everyone moves quietly. Saying out loud that you are short brings the competition running.

## The price is set when the goods ship
The part that stays out of view here is price.

Volumes are largely settled, but the actual price is said to be fixed only closer to delivery.
The buyer has locked the quantity and not the cost.
A normal contract ties the two together. Right now the seller has the power to leave price for later.
For a device maker that has to model 2027 costs today, holding an allocation is not by itself a reason to relax.

## NAND is not the same picture as DRAM
The original post puts DRAM and NAND on one line and calls both sold out. That is where readings part.

@@REF@@DRAM buyers face two more years of scarcity as NAND tilts toward surplus, TrendForce outlook (TechTimes, 2026-07-31)|https://www.techtimes.com/articles/322399/20260731/dram-buyers-face-two-more-years-scarcity-nand-tilts-toward-surplus.htm|https://d.techtimes.com/en/full/470721/micron-232-layer-nand-manufacturing.png

In its July 30 outlook TrendForce saw the DRAM balance deteriorating further through 2027.
NAND, by contrast, could swing to a surplus in 2027.
Taller stacks are the reason: SK hynix V8 at 321 layers, Samsung V9 above 290, Kioxia BiCS10 at 332 layers all pull more capacity out of the same fab.

@@CMP@@Serenity's reading|You cannot call something a glut when it is already sold out. The shortage is deepening, not easing.|TrendForce's reading|True for DRAM. NAND gains capacity from taller stacks and may run long in the second half of 2027.
The same sold out fact splits depending on whether you look only at DRAM or count NAND as well.

## The split comes in NAND in late 2027
On DRAM the two readings do not fight. The fight is over NAND.

TrendForce attached a condition of its own. If AI agents spread quickly and start parking their conversation histories on storage, the added NAND capacity may simply be absorbed.
In that case the swing to surplus never arrives.

If NAND turns long in the second half of 2027, this sold out moment was a DRAM story all along. If it stays short, memory moved as one.
Either way the buyer is left holding volume without holding price.

Google has put its name on the HBF standards alliance led by SK hynix and SanDisk.
On the same day, the alliance published its first technical specification.

@@REF@@SanDisk and SK hynix release the first OCP technical specification for High Bandwidth Flash (SanDisk press release, 2026-08-03)|https://investor.sandisk.com/news-releases/news-release-details/sandisk-and-sk-hynix-advance-global-standardization-high|https://mms.businesswire.com/media/20260803297696/en/2866619/22/sd-hbf-press-release_073026_v1.jpg

The release names four contributors: SanDisk, SK hynix, Google and Tenstorrent.
Tenstorrent designs its own AI accelerator chips.

Nvidia is not on the list.

## Why put NAND next to a GPU

@@IMG@@https://upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/2/2c/USB_flash_drive.JPG/500px-USB_flash_drive.JPG|The chip inside a USB stick is NAND. Cut the power and the contents stay put.|Nrbelex · CC BY-SA 3.0|https://commons.wikimedia.org/wiki/File:USB_flash_drive.JPG

NAND is the chip that holds the photos on your phone and the files on your laptop.
It keeps data without power, and in exchange it is slower than DRAM.
That is why NAND has lived in the storage slot rather than beside the GPU.
The seat next to the GPU only had to be fast, and HBM, which is DRAM stacked in layers, was sitting in it.
HBF proposes stacking NAND in that same seat instead.

It is slower, and it holds far more.
The premise is that what runs short when you serve an AI model is not only speed but somewhere to put things.

@@IMG@@https://upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/3/3e/DDR5_SDRAM_%28with_scale%29_IMGP6298_smial_wp.jpg/960px-DDR5_SDRAM_%28with_scale%29_IMGP6298_smial_wp.jpg|A DRAM stick for a server. ## What the specification stakes out

The Korea Times reports that the specification uses UCIe as the road connecting HBF to the processor.
UCIe is a shared standard for linking chip pieces made by different companies inside one package.

That choice says what kind of part this is meant to be.
Not a component fitted to one accelerator maker's design, but one that anyone can bolt onto the side of their own chip.

## The seat Nvidia left empty

@@CMP@@Nvidia's reading|If more bandwidth is needed, enterprise SSDs are enough. There is no reason to bring a new standard inside the package.|The alliance's reading|As inference grows, what runs short is room, not speed. An SSD sits outside the package, and that distance costs time.

Faced with the same need, one side sees it solved by parts that already exist, the other sees a seat that has to be built.

@@REF@@SanDisk and SK hynix join forces to standardize High Bandwidth Flash, a NAND-based alternative to HBM, at 8-16x the capacity of DRAM (Tom's Hardware, 2025-08-07)|https://www.tomshardware.com/tech-industry/sandisk-and-sk-hynix-join-forces-to-standardize-high-bandwidth-flash-memory-a-nand-based-alternative-to-hbm-for-ai-gpus-move-could-enable-8-16x-higher-capacity-compared-to-dram|https://cdn.mos.cms.futurecdn.net/VNoTXazt4WuxtkoAy3VWmg-2560-80.jpg

When the alliance first formed in August 2025, Tom's Hardware reported that HBF was aiming to hold 8 to 16 times what HBM holds at comparable cost.
If the cost is the same and the room is several times larger, the company with the strongest reason to push this standard is the one that keeps its own models parked in its own data centres and runs them all day.
That is the seat Google walked into first.

## Google and Tenstorrent step forward in 2026

The alliance was formed in February 2026 and produced its first specification six months later.
For standards work, that is unusually quick.

The author writes that SK hynix is more proactive on HBF than Samsung.
Even so, he expects both to show samples and begin customer qualification in the second half of this year.

The empty seat where Nvidia would be is both this standard's weakness and its reason for existing.
If the company holding most of the accelerator market does not use it, volume never arrives.
At the same time, carving out one memory slot that company does not get to define is exactly why Google and Tenstorrent walked in.
Whether the document turns into a product shows up in the samples and the qualification runs this half.
meru-fima-repo-upsize-bessent-warsh:
The US Treasury Secretary has publicly asked the Federal Reserve to enlarge one of its windows.
It is the FIMA repo window, where foreign central banks pledge the US Treasuries they already own and borrow dollars against them.

@@REF@@Bessent ready to repeat joint yen intervention, urges bigger Fed backstop (Reuters, 2026-08-02)|https://ca.finance.yahoo.com/news/bessent-ready-repeat-joint-yen-004023739.html|https://s.yimg.com/lo/mysterio/api/E6FE7F349F51E9150DEFC421DE4EDD63F06ABD194A887E45CBAD6604DD258AA5/subgraphmysterio/resizefill_w1200_h800;quality_80;format_webp/https:%2F%2Fmedia.zenfs.com%2Fen%2Freuters.com%2F4225abb81565f92c9a9bf21857ed0b8c

Reuters carried the post Scott Bessent put on X on August 2.
One line in it reads that the FIMA Repo Facility is an important backstop and that he would encourage it to be upsized in the coming months.
In the same post he said Treasury would not hesitate to take part in further joint intervention.

It was the lender, not the borrower, who asked first for the ceiling to be lifted.

## Why not simply sell the bonds

Making the yen stronger means selling dollars and buying yen.
The question is where those dollars come from.
Until now Japan's method was to sell the US Treasuries it holds into the market.
Selling bonds pushes their price down, and a lower price means a higher yield.
That long yield is the number Washington watches most closely.

The joint intervention of July 31 did not use that method.
The Treasury sold euros sitting in its Exchange Stabilization Fund and bought yen with them, so no US government bonds reached the market.

@@REF@@Japan and US confirm rare joint intervention to prop up yen (Al Jazeera, 2026-08-03)|https://www.aljazeera.com/economy/2026/8/3/japan-and-us-confirm-rare-joint-intervention-to-prop-up-yen|https://www.aljazeera.com/wp-content/uploads/2026/08/2026-08-02T233755Z_609247456_RC2NQMATKU91_RTRMADP_3_JAPAN-YEN-1785717755.jpg?resize=1920%2C1440

According to Al Jazeera, Japan's finance ministry confirmed the operation, saying it had countered excessive volatility and disorderly movements in the yen, and added that it would not hesitate to conduct further joint intervention.
After the operation the yen firmed to around 155 per dollar, its strongest in nearly three months.
The part about Japan planning to use the FIMA window comes from the original post, and English language reporting has not confirmed it yet.

## Collateral is abundant, the ceiling is not

@@BAR@@FIMA repo limit per country|$60bn|600|US Treasuries held by Japan|$1.14tn|11400@@The collateral that could be pledged dwarfs the window it would go through, and that gap is where the call to widen it comes from.@@Retrieved 2026-08-04 · limit from the Federal Reserve announcement of 2021-07-28 · Japan's holdings from US Treasury TIC data as of end-May, as cited by Reuters

There is no shortage of bonds to pledge.
What is capped is the amount that can actually be drawn, a little above five percent of that collateral.

Al Jazeera reported that Tokyo may have spent around $59bn in this intervention.
If that estimate holds, a single operation nearly empties one country's window.

## The Fed, not the Treasury, holds the switch

@@REF@@Establishment of the standing FIMA repurchase agreement facility (Federal Reserve, 2021-07-28)|https://www.federalreserve.gov/newsevents/pressreleases/monetary20210728b.htm|https://www.federalreserve.gov/images/social-media/social-default-image-opengraph.jpg

The window opened as a temporary measure in March 2020 and became a standing facility in July 2021.
The terms the Fed published then include a limit of $60 billion per counterparty.
Changing those terms requires approval from the Federal Open Market Committee.
However strongly a Treasury Secretary recommends it, the decision is made inside the central bank.

One thing sits in the way.
FIMA repo is a device that enlarges the Fed's balance sheet.
When Japan pledges bonds and draws dollars, those bonds land on the Fed's asset side while the newly created dollars land on the liability side.

Chair Kevin Warsh has made shrinking that balance sheet his stated priority.
The expansion here is temporary, unwinding as the dollars are repaid, so some argue the resistance may be smaller than it looks.

## The choice in front of Warsh this August

What is now at issue is not whether Japan has ammunition left, but whether the Fed opens the ceiling.
If the limit rises, Japan can keep intervening without selling bonds, and the ceiling on defending the yen is set by Washington's approval rather than by Japan's reserves.
If it stays, intervention goes back to selling Treasuries, and the US long yield pays for it.
Once defending a currency becomes a joint enterprise of two governments, reading the yen from Tokyo alone stops being enough.

The largest single-stock leveraged and inverse ETF pool in the world now tracks SK hynix. It holds about $5.5bn.

A leveraged ETF is built so that a 1% move in the underlying index turns into a two or three times larger move in the fund.
An inverse fund does the opposite and rises when the index falls.
Count both together and you get the size of the directional bet riding on that stock, and the stock carrying the largest one in the world today is listed in Seoul.

## Where the money sits
Add up the chip-related names and about $21.0bn is parked in products like these.
Three of the top four single names are semiconductors, and the fourth, Tesla, is tied to the same story through self-driving chips.

That is as far as the original post goes.
The question it leaves open is when the money arrived, and the answer changes how the figures read.

## The money that came in during July
July was the month the Philadelphia semiconductor index fell 21%. It was the worst month since October 2008, and $2.2 trillion of market value left the index.
In that same month the chip ETF that moves three times as far took in $6.9bn, the largest monthly intake since the fund was created.

@@REF@@Chip ETFs draw record inflows in worst month since 2008 (Benzinga, 2026-07-20)|https://www.benzinga.com/markets/tech/26/07/60550501/chip-etfs-record-inflows-worst-month-since-2008|https://cdn.benzinga.com/cdn-cgi/image/width=1200,height=800,fit=crop/files/images/story/2026/07/20/AI-chips.jpg

Buying into a fall is an ordinary decision.
Doing it through a fund with a multiple attached changes the arithmetic.

## What multiplying down does
Measured from 22 June, the plain index-tracking fund is down 25% and the leveraged one is down 63%.
It did not fall three times as far; it fell further than that.
Every one of July's 22 trading days swung at least 2% intraday, and 60-day realised volatility reached 66%, the highest since 2020.
A fund like this resets its multiple back to the starting figure at each close, and in that reset the loss on down days outweighs the gain on up days.
Put simply, a sum that halves and then doubles is back where it started, while an account that followed the same path at three times the pace is not.

@@BAR@@Index-tracking fund|+33%|33|3x leveraged fund|+170%|170@@This is the rise each needs to get back to even. What multiplies down does not divide back up, and the choppier the stretch, the more that difference grows on its own.@@Tech Times tally · 2026-07-29 · measured from 22 June

@@REF@@SOXL slid 63% while chip stocks lost 25%: why recovering the index won't fix it (Tech Times, 2026-07-29)|https://www.techtimes.com/articles/322048/20260729/soxl-slid-63-while-chip-stocks-lost-25-why-recovering-index-wont-fix-it.htm|https://d.techtimes.com/en/full/470359/direxion.png

## What August does to the SK hynix leveraged pool
The day the index gets back to where it was and the day the account does are not the same day.
If these pools keep growing through an August rebound in chip stocks, investors are accepting that gap and betting on direction anyway.
If the pools shrink during a rebound, the record will show that more people took what was left and walked.

schiff-coldcard-2021-firmware-seed-flaw:
Over four days from 30 July, 1,367 BTC worth roughly $89 million left 4,585 bitcoin addresses.
No device was physically taken and no password leaked.

@@REF@@Bitcoin cold-wallet attack spreads to 4,500 addresses as losses near $89 million (CoinDesk, 2026-08-01)|https://www.coindesk.com/tech/2026/08/02/bitcoin-cold-wallet-attack-spreads-to-4-500-addresses-as-losses-near-usd89-million|https://cdn.sanity.io/images/s3y3vcno/production/6c28c3dcd5461d3803d6e6200f1da0686dde993f-1920x1082.jpg

The cause was a single Coldcard firmware release from March 2021.

@@TIME@@2021-03|Coldcard firmware routes part of seed generation through a software randomiser instead of the hardware one|2026-07-30|First wave: 1,083 BTC out of 1,196 addresses in 41 minutes|2026-08-01|A third wave is identified, bringing the count to 4,585 addresses and 1,367 BTC|2026-08-03|Some holders move coins from self-custody back onto exchanges@@Five years separate the moment the keys were made weak from the moment they were opened. Nothing in between would have told the owner of the device.@@Retrieved 2026-08-04 · CoinDesk (tracking by Galaxy Research) · IG

## What breaks when the randomness is weak

A hardware wallet treats staying off the internet as its safety catch.
The key never leaves the device, so the reasoning goes, there is no path for anyone to take it.

That reasoning holds only if the key was made in a way nobody can guess at.
A wallet's key comes from a set of words called a seed phrase, and those words are drawn by a random number generator inside the device.
The March 2021 firmware on some Coldcard Mk2 and Mk3 units ran part of that step through a software randomiser rather than the dedicated hardware one.
That shrinks the number of keys the device can possibly produce.
An attacker never has to touch the device: generate the whole reduced set at home, then check which of those addresses holds coins.

Being offline does no work at all against that.

## Fixing the firmware does not change the seed

The headline the author passed along counts 1,200 addresses.
By the time Galaxy Research had counted all three waves the figure was 4,585.

What matters more than the count is the way the flaw persists.
Firmware can be patched, but a seed phrase already produced by that firmware stays exactly as it is.
So an owner of an affected device is not made safe by updating; the coins have to move to a wallet generated fresh.
That is where the five-year gap comes from.

## The question Coldcard leaves is not about self-custody

Peter Schiff is a long-standing bitcoin sceptic who also runs a bullion dealer.
It is worth reading the context in which he passed this story on.

IG's write-up of the same event points somewhere else.
Security researchers do not read this as evidence that self-custody is inherently riskier than leaving coins with an exchange.
The two carry different categories of risk. Self-custody carries firmware defects and user error; exchange custody carries insolvency and frozen withdrawals.

A fund that lost 67% in the month of July is still up 80% for the year.
Both numbers belong to Situational Awareness, the hedge fund built around AI infrastructure names, and both come from the letter it sent its investors.

@@REF@@'We let you down this month': Aschenbrenner's letter to investors (Business Insider, 2026-07-31)|https://www.aol.com/articles/let-down-month-read-leopold-191821000.html|https://hermes.media.static.aol.com/media/2026/07/31/8f4c92b6-bb26-399f-8e7e-63cfafdf09a0/434abb36-39da-4c34-a2a3-5a05a901409f.jpg

In the letter Aschenbrenner wrote that the fund "came closer to permanent capital impairment than is acceptable to us."
The same letter says a single block transaction stripped out all of the borrowed money, and that every short position was closed.

## Why this fund and not another

Marc Rubinstein explains the episode through three rules Steve Cohen set out in 2021.
Liquidity, leverage, concentration.
One of them you may survive, two is trouble, and all three at once is whistling past the graveyard.

Take them one at a time.
Liquidity is whether you can sell without cutting the price much.
Leverage is how much borrowed money sits on top of your own, and concentration is how few names hold all of it.
When the three overlap, a small drop forces a sale, the sale pushes the price down further, and because it all sits in a handful of names the loss lands in one place.

Rubinstein's account of July runs like this.
The 29 US-listed long positions fell 21% on average over the month, while shorts such as Adobe rose 26%.
With three to four times leverage on top of that, the fund ended the month down 67%.
Strip out unlisted holdings such as Anthropic and he puts the public book down around 85%.

@@REF@@Aschenbrenner's AI hedge fund collapses after margin calls (Quartz, 2026-07-31)|https://qz.com/situational-awareness-hedge-fund-margin-call-citadel-fire-sale-073126|https://qz.com/cdn-cgi/image/width=1200,quality=85,format=auto/https://assets.qz.com/media/GettyImages-2263060506-300x200.jpg

Quartz reports the fund ran borrowed money as high as 400%, and that SK hynix, CoreWeave, Nebius, SanDisk and Micron each fell more than 35% in July.
The size of those falls matters less than the fact that they were not five separate companies so much as five ways of owning the same story. That is what concentration means here.

## How did the market find out

The letter also describes how the market worked out the fund's position.
"As these moves proceeded, we started to see increasingly adverse trading in names publicly associated with us."
Aschenbrenner compared it to a bank run: vulnerability begetting more vulnerability.

Where that list of names came from is not spelled out.
In the US, an institution managing more than $100 million in listed equities has to disclose its holdings every quarter on a form called the 13F.

@@CHK@@13F filings on record|5|Most recent filing date|2026-02-11|Filings since then|none@@The July book cannot be verified from disclosure. The list the market called "this fund's names" came from reporting and inference, not from a filing.@@Retrieved 2026-08-03 · SEC EDGAR (Situational Awareness LP, CIK 0002045724)

Without a confirmed list, the market is likely to guess broadly.
The broader the guess, the wider the set of names that gets sold ahead of the seller.

## Why blown-up managers raise money again

What Rubinstein's piece is really about is not the collapse but what comes after it.
The trader John Arnold used to hold that "the optimal number of past blow ups was one" when hiring.
Someone who has been broken once, in that view, beats someone who never has.

The record points the same way.
Citadel's Ken Griffin was down 55% in 2008 and TCI's Chris Hohn 43% in the same year, and both survived.
After LTCM failed in 1998, the fund John Meriwether started next grew to $2.7 billion.

@@CMP@@The common reading|No one hands money back to a manager who lost 67% in a month. A hit like that ends a career.|Rubinstein's reading|The record shows managers who blew up large raised fresh capital with relative ease. The market counts the experience as something closer to a credential.
The split is whether you read the same event as a failure or as tuition paid.

The precedent Rubinstein calls the closest fit, though, is not a comeback story.
It is Amaranth Advisors, twenty years ago.
That fund was also shopped to several buyers before Citadel took it on,
and its star trader was two years into the job.

A month before the collapse, the Wall Street Journal sent a reporter to his home for a profile.
Aschenbrenner was profiled by the same paper in June.

The fund that Amaranth's trader started next drew $800 million of commitments and never got off the ground.

## So what settles it

The question comes down to one thing.
Whether this was one manager's accident, or a structural problem with all the money crowded into AI infrastructure names.

What settles it is the record without leverage.
The fund says it will now run its public book on a fully-paid-for basis.
If the same names hold up from here, July's fall was made by borrowed money. If they slide anyway, the problem was the selection.

67% and 80% are the same fund in the same year.
Losing two thirds of the capital in a month and still sitting above where the year started tells you how much it had been making until then.
Borrowed money multiplies the rate of gain and the rate of loss by the same factor.

Utilization is currently estimated at 70 to 80%, and industry accounts say the order backlog and the state of contract talks make hitting that target all but certain.
Lines that sat below 50% from 2024 would be full again after roughly a year.

@@REF@@Samsung Electronics Announces Second Quarter 2026 Results (Samsung Newsroom, 2026-07-30)|https://news.samsung.com/global/samsung-electronics-announces-second-quarter-2026-results|https://img.global.news.samsung.com/global/wp-content/uploads/2026/07/29111731/Samsung-Corporate-More-Stories-Second-Quarter-2026-Reults_Thumb932.jpg

Foundry results are also folded into the DS division alongside memory, so there is no way to check from outside whether the business has crossed into profit.

## Why does utilization matter so much
Utilization is the share of a plant's capacity that is actually running.
Think of a restaurant and how many of its seats are filled. Half-empty or full, the rent and the staff cost the same.

Contract chipmaking takes this much further because of how much capital sits in the equipment.
Depreciation runs whether the lines move or not, which is why the foundry could not even cover fixed costs last year when 4nm and 5nm utilization fell below 50%.
Run the same lines closer to full and the extra revenue drops almost straight to profit.

In a June briefing, foundry head Han Jin-man put annual profitability at 2028.
His reason was that turning one profitable quarter is not the same as finishing a year in the black.

This is where the industry splits.
Some argue the watershed for full-scale orders from large customers such as Qualcomm and AMD is not 100% utilization but whether 2nm yields clear 70%.

Yield is the share of chips on a wafer that come out working.
When yield is low, the same wafer produces more scrap, so the cost of each usable chip stays high even with the lines running flat out.
Utilization tells you how full the line is; yield tells you how much of what comes off it can be sold.

A graphics processor has to pull the data it draws with at very high speed.

meru-china-duv-ssa800-1950i-class:
The immersion scanner China says it has built sits at the same level as the NXT:1950i, a tool ASML released in 2008.
It prints 28nm circuits in a single exposure, and the generation above it, the 2015 model 1980Di, is still out of reach.

When a state-backed firm in Shanghai was reported on July 27 to have started volume production of the tool, ASML shares closed down 5.7% and fell as much as 7% intraday.

@@REF@@China begins mass production of homegrown immersion DUV machines, first units to SMIC, Hua Hong and CXMT this year (Tom's Hardware, 2026-07-27)|https://www.tomshardware.com/tech-industry/semiconductors/china-begins-mass-production-of-domestic-immersion-duv-lithography-machines|https://cdn.mos.cms.futurecdn.net/7ZotSVaMnrDA7FNSEBa4BN-970-80.jpg

Tom's Hardware reports the tool prints 28nm-class features in one exposure and reaches 7nm-class when exposures are layered on top of each other.
Deliveries run to about five units this year and roughly 20 next year.

## Why a 2008 model of all things

A scanner is the machine that writes circuits onto a wafer with light.
That single step eats 60% of the time and 35% of the cost of making a chip.

Start with the light itself. The domestic source built by Keyihongyuan runs at 6kHz and 60W.
ASML's part delivers 90W at the same frequency.

For the optics, Maolai is said to have passed validation on a 300mm large-aperture lens.
Its precision lands around 30nm, against under 10nm for Germany's ZEISS lenses, so ZEISS lenses were reportedly imported in the end.

@@REF@@China's DUV lithography still lags ASML by four generations (Asia Times, 2026-07-31)|https://asiatimes.com/2026/07/chinas-duv-lithography-still-lags-asml-by-four-generations/|https://asiatimes.com/wp-content/uploads/2026/07/SSA800.jpg

Asia Times names the tool the SSA800 and reports it was built by Shanghai Aishengna Electronic Technology Group, founded in 2023, which absorbed development teams from Yuliangsheng and SMEE.
Roughly 70% of the parts are domestic, while mirrors for the 193nm excimer laser, ZEISS lenses, vacuum chambers and synchronization control algorithms are still imported.
Turn that 70% around and it says 30% has to be bought from outside before the machine can be built at all.

## Why the 1980Di could not be copied

Huawei already held the generation above.
HSMC in Wuhan brought in an ASML 1980Di for a 7nm fab and then went bankrupt, and the Chinese government took over the company and handed it to Huawei.

In October 2025, China asked ASML to repair that machine.
The engineer who went on site reportedly found it taken apart and never put back together.

Calibration is what stands in the way.
It is a precision setting that aligns the lenses, mirrors and wafer stage down to the nanometer, fixed at the factory over weeks against hundreds of reference points.
Opening the machine throws that alignment off, and the software key that restores it sits only with ASML.

Even holding the finished product, you lose it the moment you look inside.

## What ASML actually stands to lose

China moved fast because of the calendar.
EUV was blocked from 2019, the NXT:2000i and above from late 2023, and the 1970i and 1980i from September 2024.
Ninety units of the 1980i were stockpiled just before the rules landed, but servicing that lifts performance by more than 1% was banned too, which made upkeep hard.

@@CHK@@ASML China share of sales, H1 2026|about 16%|ASML Q2 2026 net sales|EUR 9.3bn|ASML Q2 2026 net income|EUR 2.9bn@@The market China wants to win back with a domestic tool has already shrunk to about a sixth of ASML's sales. Export controls cut that share first, so what ASML newly loses if localization works is smaller by the same amount. The number points the same way the author does.@@Retrieved 2026-08-03 · sales and net income from ASML's Q2 2026 results release, China share as reported by Tech Wire Asia

## So what settles it

The question comes down to one thing.
Whether this is the first crack in ASML's moat, or a detour that export controls forced open.

The generation is what settles it.
While the tool stays at 1950i class, it is a detour.
The moment a 1980Di-class machine comes out of domestic parts alone, it is a crack.

ASML took seven years to move from 28nm to 7nm.
There is no visible reason the side walking that road again on a domestic light source and domestic lenses gets less time than that.
A scanner is the one seat in the chip supply chain with no substitute, and whoever holds it is what gives export controls their leverage.
That this tool sits at 2008 level says the leverage is still there.
meru-us-japan-joint-yen-intervention-esf:
On July 31 the Federal Reserve Bank of New York sold euros and bought yen on behalf of the US Treasury. It is the first time since 2011, fifteen years, that the United States has entered the currency market on the buying side of the yen.

Bloomberg reported that Japan alone spent 8.45 trillion yen, about $52.8 billion, on July 30, the day before. Observers put that at the largest single day Tokyo has ever spent. The yen closed Friday at 157.40 to the dollar, its strongest since early May.

What the United States added is less than a fifth of that. What will make this intervention worth remembering is not the amount but the way the dollars were made.

## A single memo caught in a Reuters photo

It started with one piece of paper.

On July 31 a Reuters photograph from a cabinet meeting caught Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent's memo in full. Under the words 'to do' was the line 'buy $5-10bn of yen'. Reuters reported that the Treasury had warned banks that morning that an intervention was possible. The Treasury did not respond on the contents of the memo.

That there was neither a denial nor a confirmation read, in the market, as confirmation.

## To buy yen you first need dollars

Making the yen stronger means selling dollars and buying yen. That requires having the dollars first, and where those dollars come from is the heart of this episode.

The money Japan uses on the exchange rate comes from the Foreign Exchange Fund Special Account run by the Ministry of Finance. It holds about $1.3747 trillion, and $1.0087 trillion of that, most of what can be turned into cash immediately, is US Treasuries. Japan's dollar wallet is filled with Treasuries. Opening the wallet means selling them, and the moment they are sold the market has more of them, prices fall and yields rise.

And the indicator Bessent has repeatedly said he watches most closely is the 10-year Treasury yield.

Selling Treasuries to hold up the yen pushes US yields up. That is the problem this intervention had to solve first.

## The ESF and FIMA, two wallets that leave Treasuries alone

What the United States sold this time was not dollars but euros.

The Treasury keeps a separate pocket called the Exchange Stabilization Fund, and it holds euros and yen. Selling euros to buy yen touches not a single Treasury.

What Japan will use is not yet confirmed. The original post expects Japan to use the FIMA repo facility. Created in March 2020, it lets a central bank pledge the Treasuries it already keeps at the New York Fed as collateral, borrow dollars for a while and buy them back later.

@@REF@@Federal Reserve announces the establishment of a standing FIMA repo facility (Federal Reserve, 2021-07-28)|https://www.federalreserve.gov/newsevents/pressreleases/monetary20210728b.htm|https://www.federalreserve.gov/images/social-media/social-default-image-opengraph.jpg

The Fed's announcement pins the collateral to Treasuries held in custody at the New York Fed and the per-country limit to $60 billion. Selling a Treasury and pledging one are entirely different things in the market. Selling puts the paper on the market; pledging does not.

## $52.8bn in a day against a $60bn window

Japan spent $52.8 billion in a single day on July 30. The per-country limit on FIMA repo is $60 billion.

Drawing the window once, all the way, barely covers one of those days. For this facility to be a way of holding on without selling Treasuries, it has to be borrowed and repaid over and over, and the dollars for repayment have to come from somewhere in the end. Pledging as collateral may not remove Treasury selling so much as push it back.

If the yen turns on its own inside the time bought, it ends as time bought. If it does not, it arrives all at once, in proportion to the delay.

## The single line that prints on Thursday, August 6

The Fed publishes its balance sheet every Thursday. One line on it records the dollars foreign monetary authorities have borrowed against Treasuries. That line reads zero right now.

If a number other than zero prints on August 6, Japan found its dollars without selling Treasuries. If it stays at zero while the yen slips again, Japan went back to the old method or stopped intervening.

Where the yen goes from 157 will be in the news all week. Nobody will write up that one line on Thursday. It is the second of the two that will still be there in a few years.

President Trump has called off the planned US attack on Iran.
His stated reason was that Iran and other Middle Eastern countries had asked him to hold off, and that the perimeters of a deal had been agreed.
That deal, he said, would include the immediate and complete opening of the Strait of Hormuz.

Oil fell about 5% within a day of the post.
West Texas Intermediate traded at $79.77 a barrel and Brent at $83.47.

@@REF@@Oil Prices Plunge 5% as Trump Halts Iran Strike Plans (OilPrice.com, 2026-08-02)|https://oilprice.com/Latest-Energy-News/World-News/Oil-Prices-Plunge-5-as-Trump-Halts-Iran-Strike-Plans.html|https://d32r1sh890xpii.cloudfront.net/news/1200x675/2026-08-02_8klqup39sh.jpg

The same report notes that the UK Maritime Trade Operations agency logged three more tanker attacks over the weekend.
Brent was under $72 at the start of July and closed above $90 last week, so this move gave back part of that run rather than all of it.

## Why one strait is this big

The Strait of Hormuz is the way out of the Persian Gulf into the Indian Ocean.
Crude loaded in Saudi Arabia, Iraq, Kuwait and the UAE leaves through that single passage.

@@CHK@@Oil through Hormuz (2022 average)|21 million barrels a day|Share of world oil consumption|about 21%|Share of seaborne oil trade|more than a quarter@@This is why Trump put a complete opening, rather than anything else, at the front of the deal. A fifth of the oil the world burns leaves through this one channel. The figures date from 2022, when the strait ran normally, so actual flows under the current closure are lower.@@Retrieved 2026-08-03 · US Energy Information Administration, Today in Energy (published 2023-11-21, 2022 data)

Put simply, the strait behaves like a valve, not a dial.
It does not taper off. It either flows or it stops.
So a single sentence about who may pass moves the price 5% in a day.

## What exactly did Iran deny

Tehran tells it differently.
Iran's Mehr news agency said it never asked the US to hold off, and Fars said reports of an agreement to split control of the strait were false.

The official quoted by Fars attached conditions.
As long as the US continues what Iran calls hostile actions, the strait stays closed, and a ship may pass only along a route Iran designates and with permission from the Revolutionary Guards navy.

@@REF@@Iran denies it asked Trump not to strike or agreed to deal to split control of Hormuz (The Times of Israel, 2026-08-02)|https://www.timesofisrael.com/iran-denies-it-asked-trump-not-to-strike-or-agreed-to-deal-to-split-control-of-hormuz/|https://static-cdn.toi-media.com/www/uploads/2026/08/2026-08-02T091335Z_1478686883_MT1ANADL0007YG4ZC_RTRMADP_3_ANADOLU.jpg

The same report describes a compromise floated by Israel's Channel 12.
Ships would enter through Iranian-controlled water and leave through Omani water, and transit fees were reportedly left out of the outline.
Oman is said to have asked for assurances that the Guards would honour it.

@@CMP@@How the market read it|The attack is off and the strait is being opened. This is the point where the war premium comes out of the price.|How Iran's statement reads|There was no request and no deal. The strait stays shut until Washington backs off, and passage is something the Revolutionary Guards grant.

Both sides are describing the same two days, and they disagree on whether an agreement exists at all. What splits them is who sets the terms of passage.

## So what settles this

The question comes down to one thing.
Is this the start of the war premium unwinding, or a pause before it goes back on.

The place to look is the ships.
If tankers begin transiting without clearing it with the Revolutionary Guards first, the deal is working. If passage stays permission-based, the announcement was words.

Oil has already answered half of it. It gave up 5% and did not return to where it sat at the start of July.
The attack being cancelled is a confirmed fact. The strait being open is not one yet.
The market has priced itself somewhere in between.

## What happened at those two companies

Most of what those two booked was not money earned by selling anything.
It was the carrying value of stakes they already held moving up.

When an asset a company has not sold rises in value, accounting rules require that increase to be recorded as income in that quarter. That is an unrealised gain.
No cash arrives, and the net income line grows anyway.

A painting on your wall getting more valuable does not raise your salary that year. Corporate accounting still writes the increase into the profit line.

Amazon added $53.4 billion pre-tax to income this way from its Anthropic stake.

Anthropic is the name that appears in both.

## So is the unprecedented AI earnings claim right

Half right.
Companies that converted AI demand into actual revenue, chipmakers and cloud operators, did post strong quarters again.

But that is not what produced the index-level surprise record.
What produced it was the book value of two companies' holdings in an AI startup.

## So what settles this

The question comes down to one thing.
Is this record the size of the profit AI created, or the price someone put on an AI company.

The place to look is next quarter.
If Anthropic is not marked up again, this quarter's gain does not repeat, and if the valuation falls the same rule cuts net income in the other direction.
If the 9.2% ex-Alphabet-and-Amazon figure holds up next quarter, that supports the reading that AI demand is arriving as real revenue.

The record is a fact. Roughly two-thirds of what made it is the value of stakes nobody sold.
A number written in by a rule can be written out by the same rule.

At 8:00 on the morning of July 28, one SK hynix share traded at 1,272,000 won. That was nearly 30% below the previous close, the lowest price the stock was allowed to reach that day.

The share filled immediately and the price was back above 1.7 million won soon after. In the Korean market that was the end of it.

Outside Korea it was not. On a market that used the same price as its reference, 960 accounts and $57.4 million were closed out in two minutes.

## Eight in the morning, when the book is thinnest

The Korea Exchange opens its regular session at nine. NextTrade, which opened in 2025 as a second venue where the same shares change hands, runs its own pre-open session from 8:00 to 8:50. The Seoul Economic Daily reported that this single share filled there rather than on the Korea Exchange.

@@REF@@SK hynix single-share limit trade triggers 83 billion won crypto futures liquidation (Seoul Economic Daily, 2026-07-30)|https://en.sedaily.com/finance/2026/07/30/sk-hynix-single-share-limit-trade-triggers-83-billion-won|https://wimg.sedaily.com/news/cms/2026/07/30/news-p.v1.20260730.9a7844d0e68446278f0d4efc939778e7_P1.png

It is the hour when Korean stocks trade at their thinnest. One price printed in a window with almost no buyers and no sellers became the day's reference.

## The price was picked up outside the border

Money is bet on SK hynix outside Korea too, through perpetual futures, contracts with no expiry. Nothing changes hands but the direction of the price, so a market can be opened anywhere, whether or not the stock is listed there.

One of the places these markets open is Hyperliquid. It is not an exchange run by a company with staff; it is a program written in advance that runs itself by fixed rules.

Whoever opens the market is a separate party. The SK hynix market was opened by trade.xyz, and trade.xyz also chose where the price would come from. It chose NextTrade.

## A seat that clears out on a 5% move

One of the rules trade.xyz set was 10x leverage: a million won of your own money carries a ten million won bet. Leverage comes with a maintenance margin line, and when equity falls below it the exchange does not wait, it closes the position on the spot. At 10x that line sits around 5%.

The reference price fell from $1,127.90 to $917.25, a drop of 18.7%.

A 5% line met an 18.7% move. There was only one outcome.

## No one broke a rule

Hyperliquid said it provides the rails and that the party opening a market sets the price rules, BeInCrypto reported. The guard trade.xyz had set allowed a 10% move at once, plus one reset, for a maximum of 19%. The actual move stayed inside that band, so the guard worked as designed.

@@REF@@Hyperliquid explains $57 million SK Hynix perp liquidations after a price feed anomaly (BeInCrypto, 2026-07-28)|https://beincrypto.com/hyperliquid-sk-hynix-perp-oracle-liquidations/|https://assets.beincrypto.com/img/9bSbOmyA4HHmwqtR8v-GH2122BQ=/1200x630/smart/filters:format(jpeg):quality(82)/2dcb42bf99444cbc8e0debfdfd30acc2

Working as designed is not the same as nothing happening. Of the $57.4 million closed out, actual losses are estimated at about $17.3 million, and 100 accounts positioned for a fall on the other side were automatically cut by $10.8 million.

Opening a market requires depositing 500,000 HYPE, about $27.4 million, with Hyperliquid. Validators can vote to burn that deposit. The burned money does not go to the investors who lost. trade.xyz said it would cover the forced-liquidation losses in full and change how it computes the price, but that was its own choice, not something the rules compelled.

## Whether one share is enough next time is decided here

What settles it is where the price comes from. If a single fill from the thin pre-open window still passes through untouched, the same thing happens again. If it changes to a blend of venues or an average over a set period, this was one operator's setting.

Where a stock is listed and how far its price travels are now two different questions.

How far that price travels is something nobody decides any more.

LPDDR is the low-power DRAM soldered directly onto the board of a phone or a laptop, and LPDDR6 is its newest generation.

Speed is written as how many megabits move per second.

## Why the top of the standard stays out of reach

@@REF@@CXMT nears LPDDR6 production: the DUV ceiling shows up in the 12.8 Gbps vs 14.4 Gbps gap (TechTimes, 2026-08-02)|https://www.techtimes.com/articles/322700/20260802/cxmt-nears-lpddr6-production-duv-ceiling-shows-128-gbps-vs-144-gbps-gap.htm|https://d.techtimes.com/en/full/471043/photo-shows-view-changxin-memory-technologies-factory.jpg

TechTimes traces the gap to how the circuits get printed.
SK hynix prints in a single pass with extreme-ultraviolet tools at a 13.5 nanometer wavelength, while CXMT layers several passes with deep-ultraviolet tools at a longer wavelength.

Layering passes means aligning the plate again each time, and a little misalignment accumulates with every pass.
That accumulated error shaves the top speed the finished circuit can hold.
The ceiling gets cut off during the sorting step, where finished parts are binned by the speed they actually reach.

China has not been able to bring in a single extreme-ultraviolet tool.
So the 11% is less a question of CXMT's design skill than of access to equipment.

## So what settles it

The question comes down to one thing.
Whether this is progress on the way to matching the standard, or a ceiling that stops just below its top.

The next generation settles it.
If 12,800 climbs to 14,400 within LPDDR6, multi-pass printing can reach the top after all, and if roughly the same 11% survives into the next generation, that is where the ceiling is.

Chinese memory has taken the route of entering on price and climbing toward the standard.
This number is the first time that road has been measured to the decimal.
It is also how the phrase "lithography is the last bottleneck" ends up written into a product spec sheet.
